title: U.S. Commerce Department Rushed to Clear Nvidia H200 Exports to China
summary:
In recent months, Jeffrey Kessler, the official overseeing the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, has pressured staff to expedite the approval of sales of Nvidia’s H200 graphics processing units to China, according to three people with knowledge of the matter. In some cases, Kessler directed staff at BIS —an agency under the Commerce Department—to approve the exports over objections from other U.S. government departments, two of those people said.

The H200, launched in 2023, is an older generation of Nvidia chips that developers can use to train and run AI models. In December 2025, President Donald Trump approved the chip, which is a generation behind Nvidia’s mainstay Blackwell product, for sale to China, after intense lobbying from former CEO Jensen Huang. As part of the approval, Nvidia agreed to give the U.S. government a 25% cut of H200 sales to China.

Revenue growth in the third quarter had fallen from its torrid pace. Privately, some investors doubted that the company could go public at the $1.5 trillion valuation bandied about for months, especially as AI-related stocks took a beating.

Throughout the month, Rao and his squad countered those concerns by highlighting growth opportunities in fields from life sciences to chip design, say people familiar with the conversations.

As for the broader market’s jitters? Ignore it, they told investors. That turned out to be decent advice: By Thursday’s close, Anthropic was worth $1.76 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

Emperors took a final sigh and slipped under the table, ministers burst while tucking into their dessert, poets quietly starved to death or choked on their own self-importance. In a public pool in Melbourne’s west, where the smell of chlorine hangs thick in the air, Dharmveer Kaur practises blowing bubbles in the shallow pool. Sounds echo across the enormous indoor aquatic centre, as people fresh from school and work mingle in the pools, spas and water slides. Kaur quietly concentrates on submerging her face in the water, following her instructor’s guidance in a lane away from the chaos.

To the young children taking swimming lessons in the lane beside her, the throngs of older men making their way to the spa, or the mother casually breastfeeding in the pool opposite her, Kaur’s bubble blowing may not seem remarkable. But for the woman who never learned to swim, it feels monumental.

title: Green Kingdom by Ben Dark review – a luscious natural history of plant life
summary:
A gardener traces the dynasties that dominate the vegetal world in appropriately sumptuous prose

John Ruskin, the Victorian writer and critic, hated the way science insisted on turning his beloved natural world into something smutty. Botanists, he complained, used “microscopic malice” to reduce the spurs, petals and stamens of his favourite flowers to “obscene processes and prurient apparitions”. Others were less squeamish. In 1908, Marie Stopes, the scientist who later became a champion of birth control, spent three days in Japan’s Matsushima Bay in a state of “grand excitement” hunting ginkgo sperms. Oliver Sacks, the neurologist, passed his adolescence at Kew gawping at the cycads’ sexual organs. Reading Ben Dark’s excellent account, it is hard not to conclude that even the most modest plants are living in a state of permanent arousal.

title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
summary:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

title: Anthropic’s IPO Triumph
summary:
Anthropic pulled it off. The biggest pure-play AI company out there, maker of the Claude line of AI models, went public on Thursday, with its shares jumping as much as 39% above its IPO price. The stock settled back a bit to close at $97.17, up 17% from its IPO price. That gave it a market capitalization of $1.76 trillion, assuming you include all options, restricted stock units and convertible notes that might one day become shares. title: BLUF: The OSS Is Back — In Name. The Hard Part Is the Authorities.
summary:
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has given the Pentagon’s top special operations civilian the most storied name in American irregular warfare. Whether the new Office of Strategic Services becomes more than a rebrand — and how it coexists with a CIA that inherited the original OSS’s crown jewels — will be settled on Capitol Hill and in the field, not in a memo.

Bottom Line Up Front

•What changed: A Hegseth memo dated Nov. 2 and released Nov. 12 gives the Assistant Secretary of War for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict (ASW(SO/LIC)) a new title — Assistant Secretary of War for the Office of Strategic Services — raises the post to parity with the service secretaries, and adds money, people and acquisition authority.

•What didn’t: Nothing in the memo touches Title 50, covert action, or the CIA’s statutory lane. The new “OSS” is a civilian oversight and resourcing office for special operations forces.

title: ‘I came close to killing Sally about six times’: how my abusive father was enabled by his fame
summary:
Like Russell Brand, my father was put on a pedestal by the media, despite a history of troubling, misogynistic comments. Meanwhile, my mother suffered through years of appalling treatment

Even though decades have passed, part of me feels I should not be telling this story. Not because it isn’t true, but because telling makes it real. And the reality is very hard to bear.

I was a young child at home in Whitechapel, east London, when my mother came into my bedroom, which was next to my parents’, and told me that my father had raped her. He had gone off to work and I was too young to fully understand what the words meant – perhaps seven or eight – and I remember being angry with her for upsetting life again, as she had done before, when she suddenly came to me at the top of the stairs and told me that they would “have to part” and that would mean taking me away with her.

title: Vincent van Gogh painting auctioned for record $190.4m after dispute over Nazi era sale
summary:
Chataigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom), which was painted in 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise, France, set a new record for the Dutch post-impressionist

A Vincent van Gogh masterpiece sold for a record-breaking $190.4m (£144.9m, A$285m) on Wednesday after a dispute between the seller and the heirs of a previous Jewish owner who sold it in the Nazi era, Sotheby’s said.

Chataigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom), which was painted in 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise, France, set a new record for the Dutch post-impressionist and became the most expensive work auctioned off so far this season.

summary:
Christian Emmanuel Sanon faces life in prison after conviction on charges arising from killing of Jovenel Moïse

A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.

Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
